title: Robust logical Bell nonlocality based on quantum error correction codes
authors: Qi Zhang, Jia-Wei Ying, Cheng Liu, Lan Zhou, Yu-Bo Sheng
abstract: Quantum nonlocality based on the violation of Bell-like inequalities constitutes a fundamental feature of quantum physics and drives the development of device-independent (DI) quantum information technologies. Existing studies of Bell nonlocality have mainly focused on physical qubit systems, where the observed nonlocal correlations are directly encoded in physical degrees of freedom. The decoherence sensitivity of Bell nonlocality largely limits the performance and security of its DI applications. Here, we investigate the robust logical Bell nonlocality based on quantum error correction codes. We construct the general logical Bell inequality in the stabilizer coding subspace and prove its violation indicates the global nonlocal feature of the logical system. Then, we indicate that the logical Bell nonlocality is robust against decoherence. Comparing with the physical qubit system, the fidelity thresholds for the logical Bell inequality violation based on the [[3,1,1]] and [[7,1,1]] repetition codes under the bit-flip error model can be reduced from 82.8% to 73.10% and 66.35%, increasing DI QKD's bit-flip noise threshold from 10.64% to 14.42% and 23.36%, respectively. Such stabilizer-based framework can be also used to characterize the multipartite logical Bell nonlocality in principle. Finally, a logical Bell test implementation circuit based on the [[3,1,1]] repetition code is presented. This work provides a feasible avenue for unlocking robust Bell nonlocality in scalable logical quantum systems and facilitates its applications in future scalable quantum network.
summary: This paper develops a framework to ensure that quantum nonlocality, tested via Bell inequalities, remains robust even when physical qubits suffer from decoherence. By encoding logical qubits using QEC codes like the repetition code, the authors demonstrate that the required fidelity thresholds are significantly improved for practical applications such as DI QKD. This provides a crucial theoretical step toward scalable, fault-tolerant quantum communication.
main_problem: The study investigates how to maintain robust quantum nonlocality, demonstrated via Bell tests, when using logical qubits protected by Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes.
main_result: Logical Bell nonlocality is proven to be robust against decoherence, significantly increasing the noise thresholds for device-independent quantum key distribution (DI QKD) compared to physical qubit systems.
method: The authors construct a general logical Bell inequality within the stabilizer coding subspace and analyze its violation under various noise models using fidelity calculations.
model_or_system: The system involves encoding physical qubits into higher-dimensional logical subspaces using stabilizer codes, specifically analyzing $[[3,1,1]]$ and $[[7,1,1]]$ repetition codes. The analysis compares the expected value of the logical CHSH operator against LHV bounds.
key_observables: Logical Bell nonlocality violation (e.g., $	ext{SCHSH}$ value), fidelity thresholds ($F_b, F_p$), and the resulting improvement in DI QKD noise thresholds.
important_parameters: Bit-flip error model parameters; specific code parameters like $[[3,1,1]]$ and $[[7,1,1]]$; physical vs. logical fidelity values (e.g., 82.8% vs. 73.10%).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the stabilizer encoding provides a local isometric mapping that preserves the nonlocal structure, although limitations exist in low-fidelity regimes due to syndrome measurement failures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $	ext{SCHSH}$ values vs. physical fidelities for specific codes (e.g., $[[7,1,3]]$), and show circuit diagrams for preparing logical Bell states using H and CNOT gates on multiple physical qubits.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework of logical Bell inequalities in stabilizer subspaces, then quantifying the robustness against bit-flip errors using specific codes, and finally presenting circuit implementations for state preparation and measurement basis transformations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the scalability bottleneck in quantum information processing by showing how fundamental nonlocality tests can be preserved across error correction layers, which is crucial for building fault-tolerant quantum networks.
